title: Health Education
description: Learn about the human body, nutrition, mental health, first aid, and how to live a healthy life.

topics.title: Major Body Systems
topics.content:
The human body has 11 major organ systems that work together:

• SKELETAL SYSTEM: 206 bones that support and protect organs, allow movement, and produce blood cells in bone marrow.
• MUSCULAR SYSTEM: Over 600 muscles that enable movement, maintain posture, and produce heat.
• CIRCULATORY SYSTEM: Heart, blood vessels, and blood. The heart beats ~100,000 times per day, pumping blood through 100,000 km of vessels.
• RESPIRATORY SYSTEM: Lungs and airways. We breathe about 20,000 times per day.
• DIGESTIVE SYSTEM: Breaks food into nutrients over 6–9 metres of digestive tract.
• NERVOUS SYSTEM: Brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Signals travel at up to 430 km/h.
• IMMUNE SYSTEM: Defends against pathogens (bacteria, viruses, parasites).
• ENDOCRINE SYSTEM: Glands (e.g., thyroid, adrenal) that produce hormones.
• REPRODUCTIVE, URINARY, INTEGUMENTARY (skin) systems.
key_facts: The human brain has about 86 billion neurons
Red blood cells live for about 120 days and are replaced constantly
The skin is the body's largest organ — about 2 square metres in adults

quiz.q: How many bones does an adult human body have?
Which system defends the body against pathogens?

topics.title: Heart Health & Cardiovascular Fitness
topics.content:
The heart is a muscle that pumps blood around the body. It has four chambers: two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).

CARDIOVASCULAR FITNESS measures how well your heart and lungs deliver oxygen during exercise.

Resting heart rate:
• Children (6–15): 70–100 bpm
• Adults: 60–100 bpm
• Trained athletes: 40–60 bpm

Factors that improve heart health:
• Regular aerobic exercise (walking, swimming, cycling) — 150 minutes/week for adults
• Not smoking
• Low saturated fat diet
• Managing stress
• Adequate sleep

Factors that damage heart health:
• Smoking (narrows blood vessels)
• High blood pressure (damages vessel walls)
• Obesity (increases workload)
• High cholesterol (clogs arteries)
key_facts: The heart pumps about 5 litres of blood every minute at rest
Heart disease is the world's leading cause of death
Regular exercise can reduce heart disease risk by 35%

quiz.q: What is a normal resting heart rate for adults?
Which activity most directly improves cardiovascular fitness?

topics.title: Puberty & Growth
topics.content:
Puberty is the period of physical development when children become capable of reproduction. It is driven by hormones (oestrogen and testosterone).

Common changes during puberty:
• Rapid growth in height
• Development of body hair
• Changes in body shape
• Development of secondary sexual characteristics
• Increased sweating (requires hygiene attention)
• Mood changes (due to hormonal fluctuations)
• Acne (increased oil production in skin)

When puberty typically starts:
• Girls: 8–13 years
• Boys: 9–14 years

Puberty is a normal biological process. Everyone experiences it at different rates — this variation is completely normal.

Emotional changes: Mood swings, new social awareness, and developing identity are all common and expected aspects of adolescence.
key_facts: The average growth spurt during puberty adds 7–12 cm per year
The brain continues developing until around age 25, especially the prefrontal cortex (decision-making)
Good sleep (8–10 hours) is especially important during puberty

quiz.q: What primarily drives the physical changes of puberty?
At what age does puberty typically begin in girls?

topics.title: Macronutrients: Carbs, Proteins, Fats
topics.content:
Macronutrients are nutrients needed in large amounts that provide energy:

CARBOHYDRATES (4 kcal/g): The body's primary energy source. Complex carbs (whole grains, vegetables) digest slowly for sustained energy. Simple carbs (sugar, white bread) give quick energy but spike blood sugar.

PROTEINS (4 kcal/g): Made of amino acids. Essential for building and repairing muscle, making enzymes and antibodies. Sources: meat, fish, eggs, legumes, dairy, tofu.

FATS (9 kcal/g): Most energy-dense. Types:
• Unsaturated fats (avocado, olive oil, nuts) — heart-healthy
• Saturated fats (butter, cheese, red meat) — raise LDL cholesterol when eaten in excess
• Trans fats (partially hydrogenated oils) — harmful, avoid

Fibres are a form of carbohydrate that cannot be digested. They feed gut bacteria and regulate digestion.
key_facts: The body needs 20 amino acids; 9 are 'essential' (must come from food)
Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) require dietary fat for absorption
Dietary fibre reduces the risk of bowel cancer and heart disease

quiz.q: Which macronutrient provides the most energy per gram?
Which type of fat is considered heart-healthy?

topics.title: Vitamins & Minerals
topics.content:
Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts but essential for health:

KEY VITAMINS:
• Vitamin A: Vision, immune function. Sources: carrots, sweet potato, liver.
• Vitamin C: Immune function, iron absorption, wound healing. Sources: citrus, berries, peppers.
• Vitamin D: Bone health, immune function. Sources: sunlight, fatty fish, fortified foods.
• Vitamin B12: Nerve function, blood cell formation. Sources: meat, dairy, eggs (vegans must supplement).
• Folate (B9): DNA synthesis; critical during pregnancy. Sources: leafy greens, legumes.

KEY MINERALS:
• Iron: Carries oxygen in blood. Deficiency causes anaemia. Sources: red meat, lentils, spinach.
• Calcium: Bone and teeth strength. Sources: dairy, leafy greens, fortified plant milk.
• Iodine: Thyroid hormone production. Sources: seafood, iodised salt.
• Zinc: Immune function, wound healing. Sources: meat, shellfish, seeds.
key_facts: Vitamin D deficiency affects over 1 billion people worldwide
Iron-deficiency anaemia is the most common nutritional deficiency globally
Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from plant sources (eat them together)

quiz.q: Which vitamin is primarily obtained from sunlight?

topics.title: Understanding Mental Health
topics.content:
Mental health is our emotional, psychological, and social wellbeing. It affects how we think, feel, and act.

MENTAL HEALTH vs MENTAL ILLNESS:
• Good mental health doesn't mean feeling happy all the time. It means being able to manage emotions, cope with difficulties, and maintain relationships.
• Mental illness refers to diagnosable conditions that significantly affect daily life (e.g., depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, ADHD).

COMMON CONDITIONS:
• Anxiety: Excessive worry or fear that interferes with daily life.
• Depression: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, fatigue lasting 2+ weeks.
• ADHD: Difficulty with attention, impulsivity, and/or hyperactivity.
• OCD: Unwanted obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours.

IMPORTANT: Mental health conditions are medical — not signs of weakness. They are caused by a combination of genetics, biology, and environment, and are treatable.
key_facts: 1 in 4 people will experience a mental health problem in any given year
Half of all mental health conditions start before age 14
Effective treatments exist for most mental health conditions

quiz.q: Mental health conditions are caused by:
options: A combination of genetics, biology, and environment

topics.title: Managing Stress
topics.content:
Stress is the body's response to demands or threats. Some stress is helpful (motivates action). Chronic stress is harmful.

PHYSICAL STRESS RESPONSE ('fight or flight'):
• Adrenaline released → heart rate increases, breathing quickens, muscles tense
• This evolved to deal with physical threats

HEALTHY COPING STRATEGIES:
• Exercise: Releases endorphins, reduces cortisol (stress hormone)
• Deep breathing: 4-7-8 breathing (inhale 4 counts, hold 7, exhale 8)
• Sleep: 8–10 hours for teenagers
• Talking: Sharing problems with trusted people
• Time management: Planning reduces last-minute panic
• Mindfulness: Focusing on the present moment reduces rumination

UNHEALTHY COPING:
• Avoiding the problem
• Substance use
• Excessive screen time or eating

When to seek help: If stress is persistent, overwhelming, or affecting daily life — speak to a trusted adult, school counsellor, or doctor.
key_facts: Chronic stress can weaken the immune system and affect memory
Exercise is as effective as antidepressants for mild-moderate depression in some studies
Mindfulness meditation changes brain structure in as little as 8 weeks

quiz.q: Which hormone is released during the stress response?
Which is a healthy coping strategy for stress?
options: Exercise and talking to trusted people

topics.title: CPR & Saving a Life
topics.content:
CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) can save a life when someone's heart stops.

DR ABC — primary survey:
• D — Danger: Check the scene is safe
• R — Response: Tap shoulders, ask 'Can you hear me?'
• A — Airway: Tilt head back, lift chin to open airway
• B — Breathing: Look, listen, feel for 10 seconds
• C — Circulation: If not breathing, start CPR

CPR STEPS (for adults):
1. Call emergency services immediately (999/112)
2. Place heel of hand on centre of chest
3. Push down 5–6 cm at 100–120 compressions per minute (to the beat of 'Stayin' Alive')
4. After 30 compressions, give 2 rescue breaths (if trained)
5. Continue 30:2 until help arrives or the person recovers

AED (Automated External Defibrillator): Analyse and shock the heart. Follow voice prompts — they are designed for untrained users.

For children and infants: modified CPR — use two fingers for infants, one hand for children.
key_facts: CPR doubles or triples survival chances for cardiac arrest
Brain damage begins within 4–6 minutes without oxygen
AEDs are now found in many public places — look for the heart symbol

quiz.q: In adult CPR, how deep should chest compressions be?
What is the correct ratio of compressions to rescue breaths in adult CPR?

topics.title: Common Emergencies
topics.content:
CHOKING:
• Mild (can cough): Encourage to keep coughing
• Severe (cannot cough/speak/breathe): 5 back blows between shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre). Alternate until cleared or unconscious.
• Infants: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts (never abdominal for infants)

BLEEDING:
• Apply firm pressure with a clean cloth
• Elevate the wound above heart level if possible
• Do NOT remove embedded objects — stabilise them
• Seek medical help for deep wounds

BURNS:
• Cool with running cool water for 20 minutes
• Do NOT use ice, butter, or toothpaste
• Cover loosely with cling film or a clean dressing
• Seek help for large, deep, or facial burns

SEIZURES:
• Do NOT restrain the person
• Clear the area of hazards
• Place something soft under the head
• Recovery position once convulsions stop
• Call 999 if seizure lasts >5 minutes
key_facts: Choking kills about 5,000 people per year in the UK
Cool water (not ice) is the correct treatment for burns — ice causes tissue damage
Never put anything in a seizing person's mouth

quiz.q: What is the first step for a severe choking adult?
options: Give 5 back blows between shoulder blades

quiz.q: How long should you cool a burn with running water?
